title: Neutron microtomography of voids in gold
author: Trtik

steps.title: Cut and drill gold rod
steps.instruction: Cut a high‑purity gold rod to a cylinder 1.6 mm in diameter and ~5 mm long, then drill a ~2.5 mm deep hole on one side using a 0.5 mm drill.

steps.title: Insert gold spheres
steps.instruction: Fill the drilled hole with four commercially available gold spheres, each 0.5 mm in diameter.

steps.title: Mount sample and configure detector
steps.instruction: Place the sample on the ICON beamline and install a ~3.5 µm thick isotopically‑enriched ^157Gd₂O₂S scintillator screen; couple it to high‑numerical‑aperture optics and a high‑performance CCD detector. The nominal pixel size for radiographs is 2.7 µm, giving a 2048 × 2048 pixel field of view (~5.5 × 5.5 mm).

steps.title: Perform X‑ray radiography at ICON
steps.instruction: Use a tabletop X‑ray source set to 150 kV accelerating voltage and 500 mA beam current; position the source ~400 mm from the scintillator screen and acquire stacks of 60 s exposure projections.

steps.title: Perform neutron radiography at ICON
steps.instruction: Expose the sample to the full white neutron beam; define the beam with a 20 mm diameter aperture located ~8.7 m from the detector (L/D ≈ 435). Acquire projection stacks of 60 s exposure time.

steps.title: Transfer sample to BOA beamline
steps.instruction: Move the sample to the BOA beamline; note that the topmost gold sphere fell out, leaving three spheres. Set the beam‑defining aperture to 40 mm × 40 mm, place the detector ~5.5 m from the aperture (L/D ≈ 138), and keep the sample‑to‑scintillator distance at ~1 mm.

steps.title: Acquire neutron projections with binning
steps.instruction: Collect projections at 225 equally spaced angular positions over 360° (step size 1.6°). At each angle record 11 individual radiographs, each 60 s exposure. Apply 2 × 2 pixel binning on the detector, resulting in a 5.4 µm pixel size and a 1024 × 1024 pixel field of view.

steps.title: Median‑filter projections per angle
steps.instruction: For each angular position, compute a median‑filtered image from the 11 raw radiographs to suppress white spots. This yields 2 486 filtered projections taken over ~5 days (the experiment was paused for a 3‑day neutron outage).

steps.title: Collect open‑beam reference images
steps.instruction: Acquire an open‑beam image set consisting of 200 individual 60 s exposures; the total exposure time for the whole experiment is approximately 2 days.

steps.title: Reconstruct tomogram with filters
steps.instruction: Reconstruct the dataset using a standard filtered back‑projection algorithm with a Parzen convolution filter (cut‑off frequency = 1.0). Then apply a combined wavelet‑Fourier stripe‑filtering algorithm to remove ring artifacts in the sinogram, followed by a 3‑D anisotropic diffusion filter (Münch) for edge‑preserving smoothing.

description: Imaging with neutrons has been utilized for number of niche applications in which imaging with other types of radiation (such as X-rays) provides less convenient probe. One such example of niche application is imaging of microstructure of some very high atomic number materials [1], [2], [3], in which radiation in (hard) X-ray regime does not provide sufficient transmission signal to reveal the inner structure of such materials. The different contrast mechanisms of neutrons with matter (to that of X-rays) allow for investigation of materials based on high atomic number elements. Objects made of high atomic number elements have been investigated using neutron imaging (i.e. tomography) already for some time [4]. It is, however, the recent progress in neutron imaging instrumentation (sub-10-μm domain) [5] that allows for imaging of representative volume elements of high atomic number materials with desired high spatial resolution. In this paper, it is demonstrated that high-resolution neutron microtomography can readily reveal voids in high atomic number materials with high spatial resolution in (for neutron imaging) affordable acquisition time. For the purpose of this demonstration, a sample of gold with artificially induced porosity has been prepared and investigated at the Paul Scherrer Institut, at ICON [6] and BOA beamlines [7] using the Neutron Microscope instrument [5], [8].
